title: Why Fear Is Ruining Your Teaching Career
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin tells an extended anecdote about a colleague, new to high school teaching, who was afraid to hold students accountable because she believed enforcing consequences would make them hate her. Despite his repeated coaching and offers of detailed help, her reluctance to follow through led to escalating misbehavior -- students leaving her room, fights, music playing during lessons -- and eventually an improvement plan and non-renewal of her contract. He uses her story to argue that fear of student disapproval is a widespread, career-ending trap rather than a minor personality quirk, and that there is no permissive, consequence-free shortcut that avoids the discomfort of enforcement. A recurring diagnostic detail he highlights is her repeated but vague reassurance that things were 'better,' which he reads correctly, in hindsight, as evidence she still hadn't actually implemented the plan. The piece's blunt closing claim is that no amount of bribery, flattery, or forced friendliness toward students can substitute for confronting and overcoming that fear directly.
points: Fear of student disapproval for enforcing accountability is framed as a serious, career-ending trap, illustrated through a colleague's real trajectory into a non-renewed contract.
Vague reassurances like 'things are better' without specifics are flagged as a warning sign that a teacher still hasn't actually implemented a management plan.
There's no permissive or consequence-free workaround that avoids the discomfort of holding students accountable -- the fear has to be confronted directly.
No amount of bribery, flattery, or forced friendliness with students substitutes for genuine accountability.
quotes: Several years ago, a colleague confided in me that she was afraid to hold her students accountable because she was convinced that they would hate her for it.
I pleaded with this teacher. I really did. I implored her to trust me and went into great detail explaining the high school plan and how enforcing accountability can be a painless process.
Sure enough, I began hearing rumblings that misbehavior was becoming severe under her watch. Some students were leaving her room and wandering campus.

If she were really following the plan, she would have said that things were tough at first and that there was a lot of pushback (because she had started so late in the school year), but she finally had control.

The truth is, there is no other way. There is no secret permissive or consequence-free strategy. There is no alternative to clear, firm, and consistent accountability. There is no hiding from the fear.
And no amount of bribery, flattery, or faux friendship with students will change it.
